title: The Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays
intro: It is the first of the Mu'allaqat in the commentaries of Ibn al-Anbari, al-Zawzani and al-Tibrizi, and every recension of the diwan its editor collated contains it, though Ibn al-Kalbi reported that the Bedouin of Kalb gave it, or its first five lines, to a poet called Ibn Khidham. The poet halts at the deserted camp of a woman he loved and weeps, then relives his escapades: the day at the pool of Darat Juljul, whose story al-Zawzani tells, when he slaughtered his camel for a party of girls; the day he climbed into Unayza's litter; a night when he slipped past guards to a secluded beauty, whom he then describes from head to foot. After that come a night like the waves of the sea, a barren valley where a wolf howls, in four lines that Ibn al-Anbari says the other narrators gave to Ta'abbata Sharran, his horse at the hunt, and a closing storm whose flood sweeps over mountains and towns. Of the opening Ibn Rashiq wrote: “In their view it is the finest opening a poet ever made, because he stopped and asked others to stop, wept and asked others to weep, and mentioned the beloved and the home in a single half-line.” Ibn Sallam reports that those who ranked Imru' al-Qays first said he was the first to do several things, among them halting his companions, weeping over an abandoned camp and calling a horse “a shackle for the wild beasts”; all three are in this poem.

translation: Stop, both of you, and let us weep, remembering a love and a home,
where the sand-ridge thins out between al-Dakhul and Hawmal,
1.sharh: He halts his companions to weep with him over the memory of a woman he loved and the camp where she lived. Al-Zawzani notes that Arabs often address one companion as two, so he may be speaking to a single friend.

translation: and Tudih and al-Miqrat, whose traces have not worn away
because the south wind and the north have woven over them by turns.
2.sharh: The traces of the camp have not vanished, because the two winds take turns: what one buries in sand the other uncovers. Some read it as the camp surviving in his heart, whatever the winds do to the ground.

translation: You can see the droppings of white gazelles in its yards
and its flats, like peppercorns.
3.sharh: The deserted camp has become a haunt of white gazelles, whose droppings lie scattered like peppercorns where people once lived. Ibn al-Anbari reports that al-Asma'i thought this line was added to the poem, though the Bedouin recite it there.

translation: On the morning they parted, the day they loaded up and left,
I stood by the tribe's acacias like a man splitting colocynth.
4.sharh: On the morning the tribe struck camp he stood apart by the acacias, weeping like a man who breaks open the bitter colocynth gourd, whose sting makes the eyes run.

translation: My friends halted their camels over me there,
saying: “Do not die of grief; bear it well.”
5.sharh: His companions reined in their camels beside him as he wept and urged him not to let grief destroy him but to bear it with dignity.

translation: My only cure is a flood of tears;
yet what help is there in a trace already worn away?
6.sharh: Only weeping will ease him, and yet he knows at once that tears shed over a ruin bring nobody back. The question is not a real one: it means there is nothing to gain here.

translation: Just as it was with you and Umm al-Huwayrith before her,
and her neighbour Umm al-Rabab at Ma'sal.
7.sharh: He tells himself this is his old habit: he fared no better with Umm al-Huwayrith and her neighbour Umm al-Rabab, loving and getting little in return.

translation: When they rose, the musk would spread from them
like the east wind's breath bringing the scent of cloves.
8.sharh: When the two women rose, musk wafted from them like the east wind when it has passed over cloves and brings their fragrance. Having praised their beauty and scent, he turns in the next line to what their absence did to him.

translation: The tears of my eyes overflowed for longing,
down my breast, until they soaked my sword belt.
9.sharh: Remembering them, he wept so hard that the tears ran down his chest and soaked the strap of his sword. The word for longing gives the reason: he wept out of sheer desire.

translation: Many a fine day you have had with them,
and none like the day at Darat Juljul.
10.sharh: He reminds himself of many happy days spent with women, and singles out the day at the pool of Darat Juljul as the best of them all.

translation: And the day I slaughtered my mount for the girls,
what a wonder was her saddle, carried away by them.
11.sharh: He recalls killing his camel to feast the girls, who then shared out his belongings and carried off the saddle that had carried him. Ibn al-Anbari takes the wonder to be at the folly of his own youth.

translation: The girls went on tossing her meat to one another all day,
and fat like the fringes of twisted white silk.
12.sharh: All day the girls threw pieces of the roast to each other in play; the white fat looked like the twisted fringe of a silk cloth.

translation: And the day I climbed into the litter, Unayza's litter,
and she said: “Woe to you, you will leave me on foot.”
13.sharh: He forced his way into Unayza's camel litter, and she cursed him for weighing down her camel so that she would have to walk. Some commentators hear affection in the curse, as in the Arab saying “God fight him, how eloquent he is.”

translation: She said, while the saddle swayed with us both:
“You have galled my camel, Imru' al-Qays. Get down.”
14.sharh: With the litter tilting under their combined weight, she told him by name that he had galled her camel and must get down. Al-Zawzani explains the verb as galling, the way a bad saddle galls.

translation: I told her: “Ride on, let his reins go loose,
and do not keep me from your fruit, tasted again and again.”
15.sharh: He tells her to let the camel go as it will and not deny him her kisses; she is a tree and her embraces the fruit he wants to pick again and again.

translation: Many a woman like you, pregnant or nursing, I have visited by night
and made her forget her year-old child in his amulets.
16.sharh: He boasts to her that he has seduced women even less likely than she is to respond, a pregnant woman or a mother nursing her baby, so she should not expect to hold out.

translation: When he cried behind her, she turned to him
with half of her, and her other half under me did not move.
17.sharh: When the baby cried she turned the top half of her body to feed him and kept the rest where it was, so strongly did she want her lover. Even a mother's instinct did not part them.

translation: And one day on top of the dune she turned hard
against me, and swore an oath that allowed no exceptions.
18.sharh: On another occasion, on a sand dune, she turned difficult and swore she would leave him, with no way out of her vow. Al-Zawzani cannot say whether this was Unayza or the nursing mother.

translation: Fatima, gently, enough of this coquetry,
and if you have made up your mind to cut me off, do it kindly.
19.sharh: He pleads with Fatima to ease her teasing, and if she means to leave him, to leave gracefully. Al-Zawzani says Fatima may be the nursing mother, or Unayza herself.

translation: Has it misled you that your love is killing me,
and that whatever you order my heart, it does?
20.sharh: He says she has grown careless because she knows his love is destroying him and his heart obeys her every command. The question form asserts rather than asks.

translation: And if some trait of mine has displeased you,
draw my clothes out of yours, and they will come away.
21.sharh: If something in him offends her, she is free to separate their lives, as easily as pulling his garments out from among hers. Some read “clothes” as hearts.

translation: Your eyes only shed tears so that you could strike
with your two arrows into the shards of a broken heart.
22.sharh: Her tears are weapons: with them she shoots straight into his already shattered heart. Another reading takes the two arrows as the gaming arrows that between them win all ten shares of a slaughtered camel, so she wins his heart entire.

translation: Many a sheltered beauty, an egg behind her curtains, whose tent no one dares approach,
I have enjoyed at leisure, in no hurry.
23.sharh: He has spent unhurried time with a closely guarded woman whose tent nobody would dare go near. Arab poets compare such women to eggs for their seclusion, their unblemished state and their pale skin.

translation: I passed guards to reach her, and a clan
eager for my death, if they could have done it in secret.
24.sharh: To reach her he slipped past guards and her kinsmen, who would have killed him if they could do it quietly; al-Zawzani says they dared not kill a king openly.

translation: At the hour when the Pleiades show their breadth in the sky,
like the spread of a sash strung with beads and gold between them.
25.sharh: He came at the hour when the Pleiades lie across the sky, their stars spaced like the stones of a woman's jewelled sash. Al-Zawzani calls this the best of the several readings of the line.

translation: I came, and she had taken off her clothes for sleep,
there by the curtain, all but a single shift.
26.sharh: He found her waiting by the curtain, undressed for bed except for a single light garment; she had taken off her clothes so that her family would think she was going to sleep.

translation: She said: “By God, there is no way to deal with you,
and I see no end to your folly.”
27.sharh: She swore she had no way of keeping him off, or that he had no excuse for coming to her at night, and that he would never be cured of his reckless love. The old narrators called this the most coquettish line in Arabic poetry.

translation: I took her out, and she walked, trailing behind us
over our footprints the hem of a figured gown.
28.sharh: He led her out of the tent, and as they walked she dragged the skirt of her patterned wrap behind them to wipe out their footprints.

translation: When we had crossed the camp's open ground and there opened to us
a sheltered hollow among winding, banked-up dunes,
29.sharh: Once they were past the tents of the tribe and in a hollow hidden by high, twisting sand dunes, they were safe from watching eyes.

translation: I drew her to me by the sides of her head, and she leaned
over me, slender at the waist, full where the anklet sits.
30.sharh: He pulled her towards him by her locks and she yielded, leaning on him: slim-waisted, with rounded calves. In another version she leans towards him when he asks her to grant him what he wants.

translation: Slim and white, not heavy in the belly,
her breastbone gleaming like a mirror.
31.sharh: She is slender and pale, with a firm figure and a flat stomach, and the skin of her upper breast, where a necklace lies, shines as bright as a polished mirror.

translation: Like the first egg, white tinged with yellow,
nourished on pure water that no crowd has fouled.
32.sharh: Her skin is white with a tinge of yellow, like a first ostrich egg, the complexion Arabs most admired; she has been raised on clean water. Others take the likeness as a pearl or a papyrus stem.

translation: She turns away, showing a smooth long cheek, and keeps me off
with an eye like a mother doe's among the wild deer of Wajra.
33.sharh: As she turns aside she reveals a long, smooth cheek, and she holds him off with eyes like those of a wild doe watching her fawn, the tenderest look an animal has.

translation: And a neck like a white gazelle's, not too long
when she lifts it, and not bare of jewels.
34.sharh: Her neck is like a gazelle's when she raises it, graceful without being too long; but unlike the gazelle's it is hung with jewellery, so the likeness lies only in its shape.

translation: And hair adorning her back, jet black,
thick as the cluster of a laden date palm.
35.sharh: Her long hair falls down her back, black as charcoal and as dense as the hanging fruit stalks of a date palm, an image of how thick and curling it is.

translation: Its braids are drawn up high,
the coils lost among plaited and loose hair.
36.sharh: Her braids are tied up on top of her head, and there is so much hair that the knots disappear among the plaited and hanging strands.

translation: A waist as slender as a plaited halter,
and a leg like the stem of a reed that is watered and shaded.
37.sharh: Her waist is as narrow as a braided leather halter, her leg as smooth and pale as a papyrus stem growing well watered in the shade.

translation: In the morning flakes of musk lie on her bed;
she sleeps late, and never girds herself to work in her house dress.
38.sharh: She is a pampered lady: musk dust is strewn on her bed, she sleeps into the morning, and she never has to tie up her clothes to work because servants do it for her.

translation: She reaches with soft fingers, not coarse, like the worms
of Zaby, or toothsticks cut from the ishil tree.
39.sharh: She takes things with soft, slender fingers, as smooth as the soft worms found at Zaby and as straight as toothsticks cut from ishil twigs.

translation: She lights up the dark at nightfall
like the evening lamp of a hermit devoted to God.
40.sharh: Her face is so bright that it lights up the dark, like the lamp a hermit keeps burning in his cell at night; a hermit's lamp burns brightest, al-Zawzani says, because he lights it to find his way.

translation: It is at the likes of her that even the sober gaze with longing,
now that she has grown tall, between a woman's shift and a girl's frock.
41.sharh: Even a grave and sensible man cannot help gazing at a girl like her, tall for her age: too old for a little girl's frock, and not yet a grown woman.

translation: Other men's blind follies have cleared with their youth,
but my heart is not cured of loving you.
42.sharh: Other men grow out of the madness of youthful love as they get older, but his heart has never been cured of loving her. Most commentators, al-Zawzani says, take the line's word order as inverted.

translation: Many a stubborn critic of my love for you I have turned away,
well-meaning and tireless in his blame.
43.sharh: He has seen off many a stubborn adviser who lectured him tirelessly about her, sincere in his advice; no amount of reproach has made him give her up, so complete is his love.

translation: Many a night like a sea's waves has let down its curtains
on me, with every kind of care, to test me.
44.sharh: Here the love poetry gives way to boasting: he has endured nights as heavy and dark as ocean waves, which seemed to bring all their worries down on him to see if he would break.

translation: I said to it, when it stretched out its back,
and its hindquarters followed, and it heaved its chest away:
45.sharh: He gives the night a body: a back that stretches out, hindquarters that keep following, a breast that draws ever further away. The hours will not pass.

translation: “O long night, will you not clear away
into morning? Though morning is no better than you.”
46.sharh: He begs the night to give way to dawn, then admits that dawn will bring him no relief, since his worries go on by day as well. Talking to the night shows how distraught he is.

translation: What a night you are, with stars that seem
tied to Mount Yadhbul by every tightly twisted rope.
47.sharh: The stars never move from their places, as if each were tethered to Mount Yadhbul by strong ropes: a way of saying that the night will never end, because his worries keep him awake.

translation: As if the Pleiades were hung where they stand
by ropes of flax to boulders of hard rock.
48.sharh: Even the Pleiades seem fixed in place, roped to solid rock. Al-Zawzani's text joins the first half of the previous line to the second half of this one.

translation: Many a waterskin of others I have hung by its strap
on shoulders of mine, broken in to the load.
49.sharh: He has often carried his companions' waterskin on his own seasoned shoulders, either literally serving them or, figuratively, bearing the burdens of his people. Ibn al-Anbari says most narrators gave this line and the next three to Ta'abbata Sharran.

translation: Many a valley as empty as a wild ass's belly I have crossed,
a wolf howling in it like a gambler with a family to feed.
50.sharh: He has crossed valleys as barren as an empty belly, where the only sound was a starving wolf, howling like a ruined gambler shouting at his hungry household.

translation: When it howled, I said to it: “Our lot is the same,
we have little wealth, if you have not yet made yours.”
51.sharh: He speaks to the wolf as to a fellow outcast: they are equally poor, two hungry creatures in a barren place. In another reading he says that his search for riches is a long one.

translation: Whatever either of us gets, he lets slip away,
and whoever sows as I sow and as you sow grows poor.”
52.sharh: Both of them spend whatever they get at once, and anyone who lives as they do will end up with nothing. Ibn al-Anbari adds that in that valley, with no plants and no game, such a life means starving.

translation: Often I ride out at dawn while the birds are still in their nests
on a short-haired, mighty horse, a shackle for the wild beasts.
53.sharh: He goes hunting before the birds have left their nests, on a huge, sleek horse so fast that game cannot escape it, as if it were hobbled. Abu Ubayda says Imru' al-Qays was the first to use this image.

translation: Charging, wheeling, coming on and turning back all at once,
like a boulder the torrent has hurled down from on high.
54.sharh: The horse can charge, wheel, advance and retreat, all with equal readiness, and it moves with the speed and weight of a rock swept down a mountain by a flood.

translation: A bay, the saddle felt slips off the middle of his back
as rain slides off a smooth rock.
55.sharh: His back is so smooth and solid that the felt saddle cloth slides off it, as rainwater runs off a slab of polished stone; a smooth back and firm flesh are prized in a horse.

translation: Lean, yet boiling over, the rumble in his chest
when his heat surges is like a cauldron on the boil.
56.sharh: For all his leanness he seethes with energy: the broken sound of his neigh deep in his chest is like a pot bubbling on the fire, the mark of a spirited, eager horse.

translation: Pouring out his speed when the swift horses, worn out,
only raise dust on the hard, trampled ground.
57.sharh: When other fine horses are tired and only kicking up dust on the beaten ground, he keeps pouring out burst after burst of speed, like water poured out again and again.

translation: A light boy slips off his back,
and he sends the clothes of a heavy, rough rider flying.
58.sharh: He runs so hard that a light boy who cannot ride slides off his back, and a heavy, clumsy rider has his clothes whipped away. Al-Zawzani takes the heavy rider to be a skilled one.

translation: Tireless, like a boy's whirligig spun hard
by his hands, turn on turn, on a knotted string.
59.sharh: His running never flags, like a boy's spinning toy whirled faster and faster as the child works the string with both hands; a knotted string, smooth with use, spins best.

translation: He has the flanks of a gazelle, the legs of an ostrich,
the lope of a wolf and the canter of a fox cub.
60.sharh: Four comparisons in one line: a gazelle's lean flanks, an ostrich's long straight legs, a wolf's easy lope and the gallop of a young fox.

translation: Broad-ribbed; seen from behind, he fills the gap between his legs
with a full tail just clear of the ground, carried straight.
61.sharh: He is deep-chested, and from behind his long tail fills the space between his hind legs, nearly touching the ground and hanging straight, both signs of a horse of noble breed.

translation: As if on his back, when he turns, there lay
a bride's perfume stone, or a stone for crushing colocynth.
62.sharh: His glossy back shines like the stone a bride grinds her perfume on, polished from recent use, or the smooth stone used for cracking colocynth seeds.

translation: The blood of the leading beasts on his chest
is like henna on combed white hair.
63.sharh: The blood of the leaders of the herd he has run down has dried on his chest like henna dye on grey hair that has been combed out.

translation: Then a herd crossed our path, its cows
like girls circling Dawar in long-trailing gowns.
64.sharh: A herd of wild cattle appeared; the white cows with their long tails looked like girls in flowing robes walking round the pagan stone of Dawar.

translation: They fled, like a string of onyx beads spaced with other gems
on the neck of a boy of noble uncles on both sides.
65.sharh: As they fled, spread out, they looked like Yemeni onyx beads, white with black tips, strung between other jewels on a high-born child's necklace, which is always the finest.

translation: He brought us up to the leaders, while behind him
the stragglers were still in a bunch, not yet scattered.
66.sharh: The horse carried them to the front of the herd and left the stragglers behind before the animals had even begun to scatter, so fast that the herd was still bunched together.

translation: He ran down a bull and a cow in one run,
one after the other, without breaking into a sweat that would wash him.
67.sharh: In one gallop the horse brought them up to a bull and a cow in turn, without working up enough sweat to drench him. The poet gives the horse the credit for the kill.

translation: Then the cooks were busy, some roasting
rows of meat on the stones, some boiling a quick stew.
68.sharh: With so much game the camp feasted: some cooks roasted meat set out in rows over the fire, others stewed it in haste in the pot.

translation: We came home in the evening, the eye almost failing to take him in:
whenever it climbed up him, it would drop again.
69.sharh: Riding home, they could hardly take their eyes off the horse; the gaze would travel up to his head and then down again, unable to settle on any one part.

translation: He spent the night with his saddle and bridle on him,
standing where I could see him, not turned out to graze.
70.sharh: Back at camp the horse spent the night still saddled and bridled, standing where his master could see him, not turned out to graze; Ibn al-Anbari says he was kept ready to ride out at dawn.

translation: My friend, do you see lightning? Let me show you its flash,
like moving hands in a crown of banked cloud.
71.sharh: He turns to a friend and points out lightning flickering in a towering bank of clouds, like hands waving. The poem moves from the horse to the storm.

translation: Its gleam lights up, or a hermit's lamps
when he tips the oil onto the twisted wicks.
72.sharh: The lightning glows like the lamps of a hermit who has just poured fresh oil over the wicks so that they burn bright. Al-Zawzani says most read the words as inverted: he tipped the wicks into the oil.

translation: I sat watching it with my friends between Darij
and al-Udhayb, and how far off was what I watched.
73.sharh: He and his companions sit out between two landmarks watching the storm build, and he marvels at how far away the clouds are; he is watching them from a great distance.

translation: Its right flank, as far as I can judge, is on Qatan,
its left on al-Sitar and Yadhbul.
74.sharh: Judging from the lightning, he reckons that the cloud stretches from one mountain to two others far away. Al-Zawzani notes he must be guessing, since no one could see all three at once.

translation: By morning it was pouring water round Kutayfa,
throwing the great kanahbal trees on their faces.
75.sharh: By daybreak the rain was falling in torrents around Kutayfa, and the flood pouring down from the hills was uprooting the tall desert trees and knocking them flat on their faces.

translation: It passed over al-Qanan with its spray
and drove the ibexes down from every ledge.
76.sharh: Only the spray of the storm touched Mount al-Qanan, and even that drove the ibexes down from every ledge, so heavy was the rain; the main storm was worse still.

translation: At Tayma' it left no palm trunk standing
and no tower but those built of stone.
77.sharh: At the oasis of Tayma' the storm uprooted every palm and brought down every tower except those built of solid stone or plaster, so violent were the rain and the flood.

translation: In the first of the downpour, Thabir
looked like an elder of the tribe wrapped in a striped cloak.
78.sharh: Under the first heavy rain, Mount Thabir looked like a tribal chief muffled in a striped cloak, its slopes streaked with water and debris. The first drops are called its nose, because noses go first.

translation: The crest of al-Mujaymir in the morning,
ringed by flood and drift, was like a spindle whorl.
79.sharh: In the morning the hilltop of al-Mujaymir stood out of the flood and floating debris like the round whorl on a spindle, with the debris wrapped round it as the spindle runs through the whorl.

translation: It dropped its load on the plain of al-Ghabit,
like a Yemeni trader setting down his bags of cloth.
80.sharh: The rain unloaded itself on the plain, which then burst into flowers of every colour, like a Yemeni merchant unpacking his bales of bright cloth.

translation: The birds of the valleys, early that morning,
seemed to have been given the finest spiced wine to drink.
81.sharh: After the rain the songbirds in the valleys chirped so loudly and busily that they seemed drunk on peppered wine, which bites the tongue and makes the drinker merry.

translation: In the evening the drowned beasts of prey
at its far edges were like dug-up bulbs of wild squill.
82.sharh: By evening the bodies of wild animals drowned by the flood lay scattered at its far edges like the bulbs of wild onion that boys dig up and gather in heaps.

1.1.1.head: قِف
1.1.1.meaning: Qifa: “stop, both of you”, an order to two companions, or by Arab habit to one.

2.1.1-2.meaning: Tudih and al-Miqrat: two more places near the camp.

2.2.2.head: نَسَجَ
2.2.2.meaning: “Wove it”: the two winds took turns over it, one covering it with sand and the other uncovering it.

3.1.3.head: الرِّئم
3.1.3.meaning: Ar'am: pure white gazelles; the singular is ri'm.

4.2.4-5.meaning: “A splitter of colocynth”: a man breaking open the bitter gourd for its seeds, whose eyes run from it.

6.2.6.head: المُعَوَّل
6.2.6.meaning: Mu'awwal: a place to wail, or something to rely on.

7.1.3-4.meaning: Umm al-Huwayrith: a woman he loved before; Hisham ibn al-Kalbi names her as Hirr, mother of al-Harith ibn Husayn of the tribe of Kalb.

8.2.2.meaning: Saba: the east wind, which blows from where the sun rises.

9.2.6.head: المِحمَل
9.2.6.meaning: Mihmal: the strap of a sword.

10.2.4-5.head: دارَة جُلجُل
10.2.4-5.meaning: Darat Juljul: a pool; al-Zawzani tells how the poet hid there, took the clothes of the bathing girls and would not return them until they came out of the water.

11.2.4.head: الكور
11.2.4.meaning: Kur: a camel saddle with its gear; another reading has rahl, saddle.

13.1.5.head: عُنَيزَة
13.1.5.meaning: Unayza: his cousin, the beloved of the poem; some say it was a nickname and her name was Fatima.

14.1.4.head: الغَبيط
14.1.4.meaning: Ghabit: a kind of saddle, or a camel litter.

15.2.5.meaning: Mu'allal: tasted again and again; or, read mu'allil, beguiling.

16.2.4.head: التَّميمَة
16.2.4.meaning: Tama'im: amulets hung on a child against harm.

19.1.1.head: فاطِمَة
19.1.1.meaning: “O Fatima”, the name shortened in the call.

22.2.3.head: الأَعشار
22.2.3.meaning: A'shar: shards; or tenths, the shares of a camel divided by lot.

24.2.4.head: أَسَرَّ
24.2.4.meaning: Keep secret, or, since the word has both senses, make public.

25.2.3.head: الوِشاح
25.2.3.meaning: Wishah: a sash of two strings of pearls and gems worn across the body.

26.2.5.meaning: Mutafaddil: someone wearing a single garment.

28.1.3.head: مَشى
28.1.3.meaning: “She walked”: the reciter's word, as in al-A'lam's recension and one manuscript of al-Zawzani, whose editors think it is what he meant; al-Zawzani's text has amshi, “I walked”, and Ibn al-Anbari's and al-Tibrizi's fa-qumtu biha amshi.

28.2.5.meaning: Murahhal: figured with a pattern like camel saddles.

29.2.5.head: الحِقف
29.2.5.meaning: Hiqaf: curving ridges of sand; another reading has qifaf, rough high ground.

30.2.4-5.meaning: “Well watered where the anklet sits”: full in the leg.

31.2.3.head: السَّجَنجَل
31.2.3.meaning: Sajanjal: a mirror, a Byzantine word taken into Arabic.

32.1.1.head: البِكر
32.1.1.meaning: Bikr: the first of its kind, here the first egg an ostrich lays.

33.2.4.head: وَجرَة
33.2.4.meaning: Wajra: a place known for its wild deer.

35.2.2.head: القِنو
35.2.2.meaning: Qinw: a cluster of dates on its stalk.

38.2.4.head: اِنتَطَقَ
38.2.4.meaning: Tie a belt round the waist to work.

39.2.1.head: الأُسروع
39.2.1.meaning: Asari': soft worms found in damp ground, to which Arabs compared slender fingers.

39.2.5.head: الإِسحِل
39.2.5.meaning: Ishil: a tree with straight, slender twigs used as toothsticks.

40.2.4.head: المُتَبَتِّل
40.2.4.meaning: Mutabattil: a hermit who has cut himself off for God.

41.2.5.head: الدِّرع
41.2.5.meaning: Dir': a woman's shift; the mijwal that follows is a young girl's frock.

48.1.5.head: المَصام
48.1.5.meaning: Masam: the place where it stands.

49.1.4.head: العِصام
49.1.4.meaning: Isam: the strap a waterskin is carried by.

50.2.4.head: الخَليع
50.2.4.meaning: Khali': a gambler; first a man disowned by his tribe for his misdeeds.

52.2.5.head: هَزَلَ
52.2.5.meaning: Yahzil: grows poor, as a man does when his herds die. So the reciter says it, as in the Jamharat Ash'ar al-Arab; the commentaries and the diwan have yuhzal, “grows lean”.

53.2.2-3.meaning: “A shackle for the wild beasts”: so fast that no game escapes it.

55.1.1.head: الكُمَيت
55.1.1.meaning: Kumayt: a bay, between red and black.

57.1.4.head: السّابِح
57.1.4.meaning: “Swimmers”: horses that reach out with their forelegs as they run.

58.1.1.head: زَلَّ
58.1.1.meaning: Slips. The reciter's reading, as in Ibn al-Anbari and al-Tibrizi; al-Zawzani has yuzillu al-ghulama, “makes the boy slip”.

59.1.2.head: الخُذروف
59.1.2.meaning: Khudhruf: a pierced pebble on a string that a boy whirls round his head.

61.2.5.head: الأَعزَل
61.2.5.meaning: A'zal: a horse that carries its tail to one side, a fault.

62.2.1.head: المَداك
62.2.1.meaning: Madak: the stone on which perfume is ground.

62.2.4.head: الصَّلايَة
62.2.4.meaning: Salaya: a smooth stone for crushing colocynth seeds.

63.1.3.head: الهادِيَة
63.1.3.meaning: Hadiyat: the leaders of a herd.

64.2.2.head: دَوار
64.2.2.meaning: Dawar: a stone the pagan Arabs set up and walked round, in imitation of the Kaaba.

65.1.2.head: الجَزع
65.1.2.meaning: Jaz': onyx, the bead of Yemen.

65.2.2.head: المُعَمّ
65.2.2.meaning: Mu'imm, and mukhwal after it: of noble paternal and maternal uncles.

67.2.3.head: نَضَحَ
67.2.3.meaning: Yandah: breaks into a sweat. The reciter's reading, as in al-Tibrizi; al-Zawzani, Ibn al-Anbari and the diwan have yundah, “is drenched”.

68.2.1.head: الصَّفيف
68.2.1.meaning: Safif: strips of meat laid in rows on hot stones.

69.2.6.head: تَسَفَّلَ
69.2.6.meaning: Tasaffal: drops to his lower parts. The reciter's reading, from one manuscript of al-Zawzani; the commentaries and the diwan have tasahhal, “comes down easily”.

73.1.5.head: ضارِج
73.1.5.meaning: Darij, and al-Udhayb after it: two places.

74.1.2.head: قَطَن
74.1.2.meaning: Qatan: a mountain; al-Sitar and Yadhbul are two more, far from it.

74.1.3.head: الشَّيم
74.1.3.meaning: Shaym: watching lightning for where the rain will fall.

76.1.3.head: القَنان
76.1.3.meaning: Al-Qanan: a mountain of the tribe of Asad.

77.1.1.head: تَيماء
77.1.1.meaning: Tayma': an ancient town in Arabia.

77.2.2.head: الأُطُم
77.2.2.meaning: Utum: a tower or fortified house.

79.2.4-5.meaning: Falkat mighzal: the round whorl of a spindle.

80.1.3.head: الغَبيط
80.1.3.meaning: Al-Ghabit: a hill hollow in the middle, named for its likeness to a camel saddle.

81.1.2.head: المُكّاء
81.1.2.meaning: Makakiyy: makka' birds, a kind of songbird.

81.2.1.head: صُبِحَ
81.2.1.meaning: “Were given the morning draught” of wine.
